prompt: Which lock do most ALTER TABLE forms take?

choices.text: ACCESS EXCLUSIVE
choices.why: Right. It conflicts with everything, reads included.

choices.text: ACCESS SHARE, the lock of an ordinary SELECT
choices.why: That is the weakest.

choices.text: No lock
choices.why: Every statement on a table takes a lock.

choices.text: ROW EXCLUSIVE, the same lock an INSERT takes on the table it writes
choices.why: That is the writers' lock; schema changes need the strongest.

prompt: The lesson names two things that make a schema change dangerous on a busy table. Which pair?

choices.text: The version of PostgreSQL and the speed of the disk
choices.why: They change the numbers, not the mechanism.

choices.text: The number of replicas
choices.why: Replicas follow the change; they do not block it.

choices.text: The size of the migration file and the number of indexes
choices.why: Neither decides how long the table is blocked.

choices.text: The lock it needs, and the work it does while holding it
choices.why: Right. Waiting for the lock and holding it during a rewrite both stop writes.

prompt: In the capture, four INSERTs waited although their lock does not conflict with the long transaction. Why?

choices.text: The disk was busy with the count
choices.why: pg_stat_activity showed them waiting on a Lock.

choices.text: PostgreSQL pauses all writes during any schema change, as a safety measure, until the change commits
choices.why: It is the queue, not a global pause; with lock_timeout the sales flowed again.

choices.text: The long transaction had locked every row of the table
choices.why: It only read; a SELECT takes ACCESS SHARE, not row locks.

choices.text: Their lock conflicts with the ALTER waiting ahead of them
choices.why: Right. Locks are granted in order; a request that conflicts with a waiting one waits too.

prompt: How many seconds did the ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN report in the lock-queue capture, rounded to one decimal place?
What turned a two-millisecond change into an eighteen-second stall?

choices.text: The replica refusing to apply the change
choices.why: Nothing in the capture involves the replica.

choices.text: A long transaction already holding a lock on the table
choices.why: Right. The change waited for it, and everyone waited for the change.

choices.text: The column's default value, which had to be written into every row
choices.why: The column had none; it was catalogue-only.

choices.text: Too many sales arriving at once for one processor to keep up with
choices.why: Four workers is light load.

prompt: Order the events of the lock queue as they happened.
items: A long transaction reads the table
ALTER TABLE asks for ACCESS EXCLUSIVE and waits
New INSERTs queue behind the ALTER
The long transaction commits and the queue drains

prompt: What does SET lock_timeout = '2s' do to the ALTER TABLE that follows it?

choices.text: It gives up after 2 s
choices.why: Right, and nothing changes.

choices.text: It runs for at most 2 s
choices.why: That is statement_timeout.

choices.text: It cancels the long transaction after 2 s so that the ALTER can have the lock
choices.why: It gives up its own statement; it never cancels anyone else.

choices.text: It retries every 2 s
choices.why: Retrying is the tool's job, not the setting's.

prompt: With lock_timeout at 2 s, the slowest sale took about 1.2 s. Why not 2 s?

choices.text: The long transaction ended early, releasing its lock before the timeout
choices.why: It slept twenty seconds.

choices.text: lock_timeout halves the wait for writers
choices.why: No such rule.

choices.text: The sales started a second after the ALTER began waiting
choices.why: Right. They waited from their start until the ALTER gave up.

choices.text: load.py rounds latencies down
choices.why: It prints one decimal of milliseconds.

prompt: Which setting would have ended, after a set time, the forgotten BEGIN of section 03?

choices.text: lock_timeout
choices.why: That limits waiting for a lock.

choices.text: idle_in_transaction_session_timeout
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: deadlock_timeout
choices.why: That decides when deadlock checks run.

choices.text: statement_timeout
choices.why: An idle session is running no statement.

prompt: After ADD COLUMN printed_at timestamptz DEFAULT clock_timestamp(), the filenode changed from 16395 to 16418. What does that show?

choices.text: The column was stored in a separate table
choices.why: Columns live in the table's rows.

choices.text: The table was moved to another disk
choices.why: Same tablespace, new file.

choices.text: A rewrite
choices.why: Right: every row needed its own value.

choices.text: An index was added
choices.why: An index has its own filenode; the table's changed.

prompt: Why did ADD COLUMN printed boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false take 2 ms on two million rows?

choices.text: The column was added only to the replica
choices.why: Schema changes go to the primary.

choices.text: The table was empty at that moment, because the earlier rewrite had moved its rows
choices.why: It had two million rows.

choices.text: A constant default is kept in the catalogue, so no row is written
choices.why: Right, since PostgreSQL 11.

choices.text: Booleans take no space
choices.why: They take a byte; the point is that none is written.

prompt: Match each change to how long it holds ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on a large table.

pairs.left: add a column with a volatile default
SET NOT NULL with no valid check

pairs.right: a rewrite and its indexes rebuilt

prompt: What does a plain CREATE INDEX block while it builds?

choices.text: Writes to the table
choices.why: Right. It holds SHARE, which lets reads through.

choices.text: Other databases
choices.why: Locks are per table.

choices.text: Nothing, because indexes are built in the background by a separate process
choices.why: That is CONCURRENTLY, and even it is not a background job.

choices.text: Reads of the table
choices.why: SHARE does not conflict with ACCESS SHARE.

prompt: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY took 5.1 s instead of 4.4 s. Where did the extra time go?

choices.text: Writing the index twice, once for reads and once for the writes that arrived
choices.why: It is built once, then caught up.

choices.text: Waiting for the sales to stop
choices.why: Sales went on at their normal rate.

choices.text: Locking each row
choices.why: It takes no row locks.

choices.text: A second pass, and waits
choices.why: Right. Slower to build, invisible to writers.

prompt: A CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY fails on a duplicate. What is left behind, and what do you do?

choices.text: A locked table until a restart
choices.why: No lock is held after the failure.

choices.text: Nothing; a failed build cleans up
choices.why: A concurrent build leaves the invalid index.

choices.text: A valid index without uniqueness
choices.why: It is marked INVALID, not demoted.

choices.text: An invalid index that slows writes; drop it concurrently and build again
choices.why: Right. It serves no query and costs every write.

prompt: Why is a rename done in several steps rather than one ALTER TABLE … RENAME?

choices.text: RENAME needs the replica to be stopped
choices.why: Replicas apply it like any change.

choices.text: RENAME rewrites the table and its indexes under the strongest lock, which takes hours
choices.why: Rename is catalogue-only and instant.

choices.text: During a deploy, old and new versions of the program run together
choices.why: Right. A one-step rename breaks whichever version did not expect it.

choices.text: PostgreSQL forbids renaming a column that has data
choices.why: It allows it.

prompt: Put the steps of expand and contract in order.
items: Deploy a version that writes both
Deploy a version that reads the new column
Stop writing the old column and drop it

prompt: Which step of expand and contract does the lesson say people skip?

choices.text: Reading the new column, the step where the program switches over
choices.why: That is the point of the exercise; it is not the one forgotten.

choices.text: Expand
choices.why: Nothing works without it.

choices.text: Backfill
choices.why: Skipping it leaves NULLs that the next step trips on.

choices.text: Contract
choices.why: Right. An old column every version writes and none reads is the result.

prompt: Why does the backfill procedure COMMIT after each batch?

choices.text: To make the procedure faster, since smaller transactions are cheaper to commit
choices.why: The commits and pauses make it slower, on purpose.

choices.text: PostgreSQL limits a transaction to 50 000 rows
choices.why: No such limit.

choices.text: Because the sales need the same rows
choices.why: Sales insert new rows.

choices.text: Short locks, small bursts of log
choices.why: Right, and an interrupted run keeps what it finished.

prompt: During a backfill, the replica's replay_lag keeps growing. What does the lesson say to change?

choices.text: Increase the batch size so that it finishes sooner
choices.why: Bigger batches are bigger bursts of log.

choices.text: Lengthen the pause between batches
choices.why: Right. The replica needs time to apply each batch.

choices.text: Run the backfill on the replica
choices.why: Replicas refuse writes.

choices.text: Switch to one UPDATE
choices.why: That is one huge burst.

prompt: With batch = 50 000 and two million rows, about how many batches does backfill_gate run?
Why add CHECK (gate IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID and then VALIDATE it, instead of SET NOT NULL directly?

choices.text: SET NOT NULL is not allowed on a column that was added later with ALTER TABLE
choices.why: It is allowed; the cost is the scan under the strongest lock.

choices.text: NOT VALID constraints are faster to check on new rows
choices.why: New rows are checked the same way.

choices.text: The scan runs under a weaker lock
choices.why: Right. SET NOT NULL then finds the valid check and skips its own scan.

choices.text: VALIDATE fixes the rows that are NULL
choices.why: It only checks; it fails if one is NULL.

prompt: SET NOT NULL skipped its scan and still took 1.1 s. What was it waiting for?

choices.text: The VALIDATE that had just finished
choices.why: It had committed; nothing of it was left.

choices.text: A scan of the table
choices.why: The valid check made it skip the scan.

choices.text: An autovacuum on the table, cancelled after deadlock_timeout
choices.why: Right. The log said canceling autovacuum task.

choices.text: The replica
choices.why: Nothing in the capture waits on the replica.

prompt: A constraint added with the words NOT ___ checks new rows only, until it is validated.
Why does the lesson call a down migration dangerous in production?

choices.text: Migration tools refuse them
choices.why: Most support them.

choices.text: Dropped data stays gone
choices.why: Right. A mistake is fixed with a new migration.

choices.text: They are slower than forward migrations, because the database has to replay the history
choices.why: Speed is not the problem; lost data is.

choices.text: They run without a transaction
choices.why: That is not the reason given.

prompt: Which item of the checklist does the lesson say teams skip?

choices.text: Setting lock_timeout
choices.why: Important, and not the one named.

choices.text: Building indexes concurrently, even on small tables where it changes nothing
choices.why: Not the one named.

choices.text: Writing the migration in a file
choices.why: Teams do that.

choices.text: Timing it on a copy of production, at production's size
choices.why: Right. It would have caught everything else.

prompt: A team must add a required column with a value computed from two others, on a table of 300 million rows. Which plan follows the lesson?

choices.text: Stop the box office for the night
choices.why: The lesson is how not to.

choices.text: One ALTER TABLE with a DEFAULT computed from the two columns
choices.why: A default cannot read other columns, and a volatile one would rewrite the table.

choices.text: Add it NOT NULL with a constant default, then fix the values in one UPDATE
choices.why: The single UPDATE is the burst section 08 avoids.

choices.text: Add it nullable, write it from new code, backfill in batches, then NOT VALID check, validate, SET NOT NULL
choices.why: Right: every step short under the strong lock.
